content: The placenta plays a critical role in determining pregnancy outcomes. Consequently, measuring biochemical markers derived from the placenta has been proposed as a method to improve outcomes for both the fetus and the mother. This study aimed to evaluate whether clinicians' knowledge of the results of biochemical tests of placental function is associated with improved fetal or maternal outcomes during pregnancy. To conduct this review, researchers searched the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register (as of July 31, 2015) and reviewed reference lists of relevant studies. The inclusion criteria were randomized, cluster-randomized, or quasi-randomized controlled trials that assessed the use of biochemical tests of placental function to improve pregnancy outcomes. Eligible studies compared women whose clinicians had access to the results of placental function tests with women who either did not undergo such tests or whose test results were not available to their clinicians. The biochemical tests included any placental function test performed using maternal biofluid, either alone or in combination with other tests. Two authors independently assessed the trials for inclusion, extracted data, and evaluated the quality of the studies. Authors of published trials were contacted for additional information. Ultimately, three trials were included in the review: two quasi-randomized controlled trials and one randomized controlled trial. One trial was assessed as having a low risk of bias, while the other two were at high risk of bias. The trials measured different biochemical markers: one trial measured estrogen levels, while the other two measured human placental lactogen (hPL). However, one trial did not contribute outcome data, so the review's findings are based on two trials involving 740 participants. The results showed no evidence of a difference in the incidence of neonatal death (risk ratio [RR] 0.88, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.36 to 2.13, two trials, 740 participants, very low-quality evidence) or the frequency of small-for-gestational-age infants (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.19, one trial, 118 participants, low-quality evidence). Regarding secondary outcomes, there was no clear evidence of a difference between women who underwent biochemical tests of placental function and those who received standard antenatal care in terms of stillbirth (RR 0.56, 95% CI 0.16 to 1.88, two trials, 740 participants, very low-quality evidence) or neonatal death (RR 1.62, 95% CI 0.39 to 6.74, two trials, 740 participants, very low-quality evidence). The directions of potential effects for these outcomes were inconsistent. There was also no evidence of a difference between groups in the rates of elective delivery (RR 0.98, 95% CI 0.84 to 1.14, two trials, 740 participants, low-quality evidence), cesarean section (RR 0.48, 95% CI 0.15 to 1.52, one trial, 118 participants, low-quality evidence), changes in maternal anxiety scores (mean difference -2.40, 95% CI -4.78 to -0.02, one trial, 118 participants), neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) admissions (RR 0.32, 95% CI 0.03 to 3.01, one trial, 118 participants), or preterm birth before 37 weeks of gestation (RR 2.90, 95% CI 0.12 to 69.81, one trial, 118 participants). One trial (118 participants) reported no cases of serious neonatal morbidity. Maternal death was not reported in any of the included studies. Several secondary outcomes related to neonatal health were not reported in the included studies. These outcomes included umbilical artery pH < 7.0, NICU admission for more than seven days, very preterm birth (< 32 weeks of gestation), need for ventilation, organ failure, fetal abnormalities, and neurodevelopmental outcomes in childhood (e.g., cerebral palsy, neurodevelopmental delay). Similarly, several maternal secondary outcomes were not reported, such as admission to intensive care, high-dependency unit admission, hospital stays longer than seven days, pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, and women's perceptions of care. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to support the use of biochemical tests of placental function to reduce perinatal mortality or improve the identification of small-for-gestational-age infants. However, the review included data from only two studies that measured estrogen and hPL, and the quality of the evidence was low or very low. Two of the trials were conducted in the 1970s on women with various antenatal complications, and the findings cannot be generalized to low-risk pregnancies or specific pregnancy complications, such as fetal growth restriction. Additionally, neonatal mortality rates have significantly decreased since the 1970s, meaning that outcomes observed in those studies may not reflect current clinical realities. For example, an infant delivered at 28 weeks of gestation today would have a much higher chance of survival than in the 1970s, which could affect the primary outcomes of the meta-analysis. With data from only two studies (740 women), this review was underpowered to detect differences in the incidence of neonatal death or the frequency of small-for-gestational-age infants, as these outcomes have a background incidence of approximately 0.75% and 10% of pregnancies, respectively. Similarly, the review was underpowered to detect differences in rare or severe adverse events, such as serious neonatal morbidity. Two of the three included studies were quasi-randomized, introducing a significant risk of bias in group allocation. Additionally, performance bias may have been present, as one of the studies contributing data did not perform venipuncture on participants receiving standard care, allowing clinicians to identify which group participants belonged to. Future studies should employ more robust randomization methods, ensure proper concealment of group allocation, and be adequately powered to detect differences in rare adverse events. The studies included in this review examined only two biochemical markers (estrogens and hPL), but many other placental products could serve as potential indicators of placental function. These include placental growth factor (PlGF), human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG), pregnancy-associated plasma protein A (PAPP-A), placental protein 13 (PP-13), pregnancy-specific glycoproteins, and progesterone metabolites. Further research should investigate these alternative markers. Future randomized controlled trials should focus on analytes with the highest predictive reliability for placental dysfunction, particularly in relation to small-for-gestational-age infants and perinatal mortality.
